before.label: Geography & environmental inquiry
before.date_label: Nineteenth-century roots; regional, cultural and ecological inquiry
before.description: Several traditions ask how human activity and physical environments shape landscapes. Vidal investigates regional individuality; Marsh examines human environmental modification; Sauer relates physical and cultural forms; Leopold joins ecological observation with ethical concern. Their later uses differ, including Annales geography and environmental historians’ landscape inquiry.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Paul Vidal de la Blache influences Febvre and Bloch; George Perkins Marsh, Man and Nature (1864), is an environmental precursor, not an Annales founder. Additional readings: Sauer, “The Morphology of Landscape” (1925); Leopold, A Sand County Almanac (1949).

representative_people.context: Investigates how human activity forms a region’s geographical individuality; engages Michelet’s national framing. His human geography is a resource for Annales, with the reception limits retained in the connection note.
representative_people.works: Tableau de la géographie de la France (1903)

representative_people.context: Studies human modification of physical environments; a precursor to environmental inquiry, not an Annales founder.
representative_people.works: Man and Nature; or, Physical Geography as Modified by Human Action (1864)

representative_people.context: Treats landscapes as related physical and cultural forms with histories; challenges rigid explanations from physical conditions alone.
representative_people.works: “The Morphology of Landscape” (1925)

representative_people.context: Conservationist whose ecological observation and teaching supplied one model for reading landscapes; Cronon later recalls workshops modeled on his course.
representative_people.works: A Sand County Almanac (1949)

before.scope_note: Vidal’s human geography and Marsh’s environmental inquiry are different resources; neither defines all later environmental history. This is a selective set of resources for historians, not a complete history of geography. Sauer and Leopold supply distinct approaches; national framing, ecological care and landscape morphology are not a single programme.

before.label: Progressive & consensus historiography (US)
before.description: A paired comparison of influential US approaches, not one school or the whole profession. Progressive interpretations emphasize economic interest and conflict; postwar consensus interpretations emphasize shared commitments across political divisions. The labels are contested and do not capture every argument of the writers grouped under them.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Frederick Jackson Turner (1893); Charles Beard, An Economic Interpretation of the Constitution (1913); Richard Hofstadter, The American Political Tradition (1948); Louis Hartz, The Liberal Tradition in America (1955).

progressive.people: Added Libby, Parrington, Boorstin, Potter and Higham with distinct historian/critic roles. Reused Libby in geography. Preserved Mary and Charles Beard’s coauthorship and the existing Benson critic selection.
progressive.works_and_arguments: Read Beard’s original preface and selected argument, Turner’s complete 1910 address, Libby’s complete introductory apparatus, Hofstadter’s complete published introduction, Hartz’s preface and chapter opening, Higham’s complete 1959 critique, and Parrington’s foreword/selected introduction. Named works now have direct sources; original publication and later editions remain separate.
progressive.internal_distinctions: Expanded the two inherited broad strands and retained the Beard collaboration strand. Added sectional mapping/proxies, multiple hypotheses, literary conflict, critical portraits, liberal conformity and consensus criticism. Hartz and Boorstin do not have the same evaluative stance, and Hofstadter’s critical selection is not general national celebration.
progressive.incoming_connections: Added Cunningham’s methodological contribution and Libby’s mapping route into Beard with primary citations. Preserved the materialism and philosophy comparisons and the qualified New Left/Benson critiques. Higham supplies a named internal critic without a self-loop or invented full person node.
progressive.outgoing_connections: Strengthened political/economic contributions using original framing; added Beard’s critique of Bancroft and Hartz’s specific criticism of Marx. Original endpoints and types remain stable, including the two-way Beard partnership. No uniform Progressive or consensus position is inferred.
progressive.evidence_and_interpretation: Source notes separate complete short texts, selected chapters, mediated Boorstin/Potter claims and unread body evidence. Colonial and racial hierarchies, free-land assumptions and sweeping claims about national homogeneity remain attributed. Libby’s maps and Beard’s data are not replicated; Higham’s historiographical diagnosis is a contemporary intervention rather than a neutral census.
